title: Exploring residence time and movement patterns of adult Lycorma delicatula (Hemiptera: Fulgoridae) with photo re-identification
content:
Abstract
The spotted lanternfly, Lycorma delicatula (White), is an invasive pest that has rapidly expanded since its introduction in 2014. Despite its rapid spread, little is known about individual movement behavior during the winged adult stage when dispersal ability is greatest and oviposition occurs. We used photo re-identification methods to explore the movement patterns and residence time of adult lanternflies on 21 trees across 5 sites in an urban environment during the final 8 wk of the adult stage (September to November). We recorded 982 unique individuals, the majority of which were recaptured at least once. Results indicated a transition from a mobile to a more sedentary phase: recapture probability increased over time and plateaued around 0.9 midway through our study, coinciding with the arrival of a large group of individuals in early October that persisted through the end of our study. Mean individual residence time within our study system was 9 d, but varied among sites and trees. Individuals at high-density sites exhibited longer site-level but shorter tree-level residence times than low-density sites, suggesting increased within-site movements. Although most individuals were recaptured on the same tree where they had been previously observed, approximately one quarter were recaptured on different trees, and 7 individuals moved between sites, including 3 that moved on the same day, suggesting possible coordinated movement. We also estimated a population size of 10,264 individuals. These results confirm photo re-identification is effective for quantifying fine-scale adult movement and provide insights relevant to invasion dynamics and management.
